107.t: Detroit's musicians: Burrell, Flanagan, Chambers and others
107.s: Foster lists the many players he met in Detroit, from Kenny Burrell and Tommy Flanagan to Thad and Elvin Jones, Abe Woodley, Roland Hanna and Paul Chambers.
107.q: Ostensibly I was going to aid the detectives in the search for these instruments, which was just useless. They could have looked for them without my help. But I found so much going in Detroit that I fell in love with the city immediately. I met Kenny Burrell. I met Tommy Flanagan, a very young…

107.t: More Detroit names: Parky Grote, Terry Pollard, Bess Bonnier
107.s: Brower runs through further Detroit musicians and Foster says who was there, who had left and who he met later.
107.q: Yeah, Parky Grote was one of the white musicians who came around and played with -- sat in with black musicians all over Detroit. I think he played -- I’m forgetting if he played a saxophone or a trombone. Do you have him listed as a --

107.t: Hanging out with Barry Harris, Donald Byrd and the Conyers brothers
107.s: Foster's circle in Detroit included Harris, Byrd and Sonny Red, and hipsters like Nathan Conyers.
107.q: I didn’t know Conyers, but the Conyers family had about three or four brothers. I used to hang out with one of them, Nathan Conyers.

107.t: Leaders and teachers on the Detroit scene
107.s: Barry Harris, Lefty Edwards, Sonny Stitt, Curtis Fuller, Tate Houston and Billy Mitchell stood out.
107.q: At a very young age Barry Harris was one of the teachers. There was a tenor saxophonist named Lefty Edwards who to me was another -- who epitomized the hard- bop approach. His lines were like Sonny Stitt’s lines. Sonny Stitt definitely, who was a native of Saganaw [Michigan]. That’s the Detroit…

107.t: Younger Detroiters: Louis Hayes, Curtis Fuller, Leon Henderson
107.s: Hayes and Fuller were still schoolboys; Foster's peers were Harris, Flanagan and Burrell.
107.q: Yeah, because he was very young. He was one of the young ones like Paul Chambers. I really wasn’t aware of him until --

144.t: Claire Roquemore, the Detroit trumpeter, and Kenny Burrell
144.s: Fuller praises Claire Roquemore as a great trumpeter who never reaped the benefit, and says Kenny Burrell put him in musical situations.
144.q: Beautiful player. Yeah, he would give Donald Byrd, Miles Davis and all the rest of them a run for their money. He was the trumpet player that never got any significance. He never reaped any benefits from it.

144.t: Thad Jones, Pepper Adams and visiting Chet Baker and Mulligan
144.s: Pepper was Thad Jones's fan; Fuller says Pepper overwhelmed visiting New Yorkers and Mulligan and Chet Baker at the Showbar.
144.q: Hank had been gone. They factored in, too. The reason I had to speak of Pepper is because Pepper was Thad Jones biggest fan. To give you some idea of what we were playing in high school. When everybody was all, (scats basic melody on downbeats of a simple progression) Here’s what we were playing…

144.t: Sonny Stitt, Michigan talent and a hip white drummer
144.s: Fuller discusses musicians from Pittsburgh, Pontiac and Flint, and a white drummer who played with Woody Herman.
144.q: Well, Sonny married a girl from here, Barbara. He is from Detroit. He wasn't born in Detroit, he was actually born, like Paul Chambers, in Pittsburgh. I think Sonny Stitt was too.

267.t: Detroit bands compared with New Orleans
267.s: Detroit bands favoured show-style honking tenor, so Ford as a Parker-style alto player took a back seat and returned home.
267.q: At the time, yes, very definitely. They played, they were leaning toward a more, I'd say, a rock swing type, show type band. See, at the time it was like Illinois Jacket, tenor players, played like that. And I was playing alto. I was trying to play alto like Charlie Parker. So the thing up there…

890.t: Detroit jam scene: Rockamore, Barry Harris, Roland Hanna, Joe Hunter
890.s: He describes jamming with Detroit musicians, the New Orleans-Detroit connection with Marcus Belgrave, and working with Joe Hunter and Earl Van Dyke before Motown.
890.q: When I got to Detroit I never had no problem ‘cause I always knew how to govern myself for the type of job that I have. When I got to Detroit I was fortunate enough to meet Clair Rockamore, a little trumpet player. If you read Miles Davis’ autobiography you’ll see his name in there. Clair…

576.t: Is there a Detroit sound; Flanagan, Burrell and Detroit friends
576.s: Jordan says Detroit musicians are originals, naming Tommy Flanagan, Kenny Burrell, Hank Jones and Milt Jackson.
576.q: Woooah, yeah. We’re all originals. I mean most of them. Look at Tommy Flanagan. I grew up with Tommy and Barry and Kenny Burrell and we are all very close. And our hero at the time, from Detroit, was Hank Jones and Milt Jackson. Because Milt Jackson had gone off with Dizzy Gillespie and Hank Jones…

486.t: Detroit musicians arriving in New York
486.s: Later colleagues in Oscar Pettiford's band and the Detroit players who arrived in 1956.
486.q: Good question. I don’t know. A lot of guys I wound up playing with later in Oscar Pettiford’s band, the guys like Jimmy Cleveland and Jerome Richardson, and Donald Byrd. Well that was later, when the Detroit — that’s another thing — in 1956 there was this mass immigration from Detroit that took…

343.t: Detroit after college: Kirk Lightsey, Alice McLeod's jam sessions, and the Detroit beat
343.s: McBee met Kirk Lightsey in the Army, moved to Detroit, played with its drummers, and describes their forward beat, plus Tony Williams, Jimmy Cobb and Roy Brooks.
343.q: Louis Hayes. I was sort of a, until now, an adopted son of Detroit, because people seem to have liked what I did. And so I got a chance to play with everybody. And you learn that, you know, at that particular time Detroit was the place where most of the great musicians, you know, came from, you…

417.t: Gene Ludwig, the Byrd brothers, Jimmy Ponder and Pittsburgh's send-off
417.s: He recalls the Gene Ludwig trio, Jerry and Wendell Byrd, and Jimmy Ponder, and how Pittsburgh's reputation helped him.
417.q: Gene Ludwig. We used to call him Eugene Ludwig. People called him Gene Ludwig. He preferred that, Gene Ludwig. And also, Jerry Byrd and his brother Wendell Byrd. Fabulous musicians. He played the first real live jazz guitar that I ever heard, Jerry Byrd, and his brother was a fabulous horn player,…

371.t: Detroit pianists: Earl Van Riper, Tommy Flanagan, Barry Harris
371.s: The interviewer runs through Detroit pianists; Jones barely knew most of them.
371.ch: Early bands and the road to New York
371.q: Earl Van Riper? He’s a Detroit pianist. I meant Earl early on, and subsequently a couple times after. He passed away, I guess, about eight or 10 years ago, I believe. He was a fine pianist. He was one of a number of fine pianists that were in the Detroit area. Tommy Flanagan was from the Detroit…

165.s: He names Hank Jones, Barry Harris, Tommy Flanagan, Wardell Gray, Billy Mitchell and Doug Watkins in Detroit.
165.q: Barry Harris. Barry Harris was working at a place called the Bluebird, I think. Tommy Flanagan, too, was there – were there.

228.t: Prestige sidemen and the regional streams feeding New York
228.s: His habit left no musical circle beyond rehearsals; musicians from Detroit, Philadelphia, Chicago and New Jersey arrived as children of Bud and Bird.
228.ch: Bird memories, cabaret card and Prestige years
228.q: I didn’t have – my monster wouldn’t let me have a musical circle. I didn’t have no time to sit down with nobody and chat about something or do anything. It had to be about a rehearsal to do a particular project. Then we go rehearse it and do it. Then, “I’ll see you later.” I’m gone. Sometimes we…

382.t: Hemp Pie and other musicians from Pittsburgh and the Midwest
382.s: She lists Pittsburgh figures such as George Benson and musicians from Ohio, Detroit and Chicago.
382.ch: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
382.q: I don't know, I mean Pittsburgh, I don't know that they're in the business of - you had to come to New York to make a record so you had to go someplace else, you know. There's a lot of talent around Pittsburgh that should have been on records that never made it. They just didn't want to leave. I…

70.s: Buckner's solos on Lunceford's Margie were mistaken for Willie Smith; Detroit had good bands, and Buckner played xylophone with four mallets.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And, you know, around Detroit they had a lot of good bands. When I was there at McKinney's band, they had a lot of good bands. Billy Minor had a good band around there, you know. And that's where Inge came from. That's where we got Inge, from Billy Minor's band.

386.s: They name musicians from Detroit such as Billy Boyd, Don Redman and Sidney De Paris, and later Milt Jackson and Kenny Burrell.
386.q: Well, you had guys like Lanky Bowman and you had Billy Boyd, you know, the guy that's calling me every day. Billy come from Detroit and then he went with McKinney's Cotton Pickers. I think he was the youngest conductor they ever had. McKinney had a good band. Fathead and De Paris...that De Paris…
